structure.title: I. Background (A. Variation in Work Incentives; B. Welfare Reform)
II. Data (Core Sample, State-Level Controls, Supplemental Data)
III. Estimation Strategy (A. Identification Assumptions and Tests)
IV. Main Results (Employment, Experience, Earnings; A. Survey Evidence; B. Translating Earnings to Wages)
VI. Why Do Early-Exposed Mothers Earn More? (A. Mechanisms; B. Comparison to Other Policies)

observations.statement: States the estimand as the causal effect of exposure to expanded post-childbirth work incentives immediately at first birth versus several years later, identified in a triple-difference model nesting a birth-cohort comparison inside a marital-status comparison.

The identifying assumption, that no factor besides the change in work incentives differentially affects post-birth outcomes of early-exposed never-married mothers, is explicitly labeled untestable, with credibility probed only indirectly through pre-period and comparison-group checks.

Alongside the main triple-difference model, a simpler difference-in-differences event-study specification for never-married mothers alone is reported explicitly to make the identifying variation more transparent to readers.

The close timing of 1990s welfare reforms alongside the EITC expansion is flagged as a specific threat to identification, following a cited critique, and addressed by controlling for state-level welfare-policy variation rather than by a separate research design.
observations.locator: Section IB, Welfare Reform as an Additional Work Incentive

observations.statement: The analysis sample is built by linking two datasets that are each individually insufficient: longitudinal Social Security earnings records with no demographic information, and Current Population Survey responses with only a single year of reported earnings per person.

The unit of observation is a mother tracked annually across a fixed window of years before and after her first birth, with employment, experience and earnings all measured relative to that birth-year zero point.

Core sample restrictions include a maximum age at CPS interview, a minimum age at first birth, and membership in one of two birth-cohort exposure windows, each justified as reducing confounds such as schooling status or measurement error from an overly extended sample period.

Survey respondents are linked to administrative earnings records using a Census-created identifier, with match rates checked for stability across survey years and marital status, and one CPS survey year dropped for an unusually low match rate.
Social Security earnings and Numident records are restricted administrative data accessed with agency assistance and subject to a disclosure review process, acknowledged in the paper's front matter.

Each main results table reports the underlying observation count for every outcome column alongside the dependent-variable mean, and a separate summary-statistics table is referenced for the full analysis sample.

Treatment is an indicator for having a first birth in the cohort window exposed at or near the reform, interacted with never-married status to isolate the high-impact group targeted by the incentive change.

Employment is defined from an indicator for positive total earnings in administrative records; work experience is then constructed as a running sum of estimated annual employment impacts rather than measured directly.
observations.locator: Section II; Section IV, Work Experience

observations.statement: All dollar values, including earnings, EITC benefit levels and later welfare-policy variables, are converted to a common real base year using the Consumer Price Index.

Marital status, race, education and other demographics are assigned at the time of the CPS survey rather than at first birth, which the paper identifies as a source of measurement error most concerning for the marital-status treatment assignment.

A mechanism test constructs four mutually exclusive indicators crossing high or low earnings with high or low early post-birth employment, using a within-year earnings percentile cutoff and an employment-in-each-of-several-years experience definition.

Survey-based hours and weeks of work from the CPS are converted into an implied full-time-full-year years-of-experience measure using a standard weekly-hours and annual-weeks benchmark, cross-checked against the administrative experience construct.

The main results table's notes restate the full fixed-effect and control set, describe how control effects are allowed to differ by marital status, and state the clustering level, repeating information rather than leaving it only in the surrounding text.
Both main outcome tables report the dependent-variable mean and the observation count directly beneath the coefficient rows for every outcome column.

The baseline specification is a fully dynamic event-study regression, which is then collapsed into a small number of post-birth period interactions (short, medium and long run) as the summary specification reported in the main results table.

Standard errors are clustered at the state level throughout, but the paper states this choice as a fact of the specification without an accompanying explicit rationale for why the state is the appropriate clustering unit.
observations.locator: Section III, end of specification paragraph
observations.quote: For all analyses, we include standard errors clustered at the state level.

observations.statement: As a complement to state-clustered standard errors, the paper also reports confidence intervals built from randomization inference to address concerns about correlated shocks across states, presented as an alternative rather than a replacement for clustering.
observations.locator: Section III; Section V, Randomization Inference

observations.statement: Pre-birth coefficients in the single-group, difference-in-differences and triple-difference event studies are presented directly in the main results figure as the primary pre-trend check.

A second pre-trend style check tests whether the timing of the improvement in never-married mothers' outcomes lines up with the reform date, described as passing in the main text with full supporting results placed in the online appendix.

A covariate-balance style comparison shows that never-married and married mothers experienced similar or smaller changes in observable characteristics across the early- and late-exposed cohorts, offered as support for the comparison-group choice, with the underlying figure placed in the online appendix.
observations.locator: Section IIIA, Comparability of Married and Never-Married Mothers

observations.statement: Childless women are assigned placebo birth years drawn from the distribution of actual birth years among never-married mothers, and the same triple-difference specification is applied to this placebo sample as a falsification exercise summarized in a dedicated figure.
observations.locator: Section V, Childless and Lower-Income Comparison Groups; Figure 4

observations.statement: Selective marriage and CPS-linkage timing are treated as attrition-like threats, tested using a separate survey's marital histories and by checking whether the gap in characteristics between cohorts widens as the CPS survey occurs further from first birth.
observations.locator: Section IIIA, Selection into Being Single and Measurement Error

observations.statement: Robustness to the choice of comparison group is assessed by rerunning the main specification against several alternative lower-earning or childless comparison groups, plotting all resulting long-run estimates together against each group's own average outcome level.
observations.locator: Section V, Childless and Lower-Income Comparison Groups; Figure 4

observations.statement: A calendar-year event-study specification, comparing early- and late-exposed mothers within the same calendar year rather than by years since birth, is used as an alternative timing structure to probe annual confounds, with detailed figures placed in the online appendix.

Robustness to more flexible controls for economic conditions, including letting welfare and unemployment effects vary by child age and adding state-year fixed effects, is summarized in the main text with the full underlying tables placed in the online appendix.
observations.locator: Section V, Alternative Controls for Economic Conditions

observations.statement: A further robustness battery covers propensity-score weighting, letting age effects vary with age at first birth, adding individual fixed effects, and restricting to CPS household heads; the main text summarises the battery in one sentence and places the full tables in the online appendix.

Alternative sample restrictions vary how many years after birth a mother must be observed in the CPS and drop older mothers whose children may have already left home, testing for trends consistent with selective survival into the sample.

Randomization inference, built by repeatedly assigning a placebo early-exposure indicator to randomly drawn birth cohorts, is used as a final check on the main long-run earnings result, with the resulting placebo distribution shown in the online appendix.

Long-run effects are estimated separately by finer birth-cohort groups defined by the child's age at exposure, to test whether experience and earnings impacts scale with how early in a child's life the incentive arrived.
observations.locator: Section VIA; online Appendix Figures A.14-A.15

observations.statement: The paper explicitly flags that estimates from the finer cohort-by-exposure-age splits are imprecise, so a dose-response or nonlinear pattern in returns to experience cannot be confirmed and alternative explanations for deviations cannot be ruled out.
observations.locator: Section VIA, footnote on the dose-response figure

observations.statement: Survey-based hours and weeks of work serve as an intermediate outcome that cross-validates the administrative-earnings-based experience measure, since the administrative data alone cannot capture intensive-margin hours responses.
observations.locator: Section IVA, Survey Evidence on Hours of Work

observations.statement: A direct mechanism test regresses joint high/low earnings by high/low early-experience indicators on treatment, checking whether earnings gains concentrate among mothers who were also induced into more post-birth work experience rather than appearing broadly.

Self-employment income, hours-of-work, and fertility or marriage-timing channels are each examined as alternative explanations for the earnings pattern, including a specification restricted to wage employment and estimates for fertility and marriage outcomes.
observations.locator: Section IVB; Section VIA, Other Channels

observations.statement: A higher-return-to-experience-through-occupation-change channel is explored using CPS occupation categories, but the evidence is explicitly described as imprecise and unable to explain much of the overall earnings increase even taken at face value.
observations.locator: Section VIA, Higher Return to Experience

observations.statement: Long-run earnings and employment effects are consistently interpreted as a share of late-exposed mothers' own average outcome level rather than only reported as raw levels, both in the text discussion and along a comparison-group figure axis.

The paper's preferred summary magnitude is an implied annual return to a year of work experience, computed by dividing the estimated earnings effect by the estimated experience effect rather than reporting either coefficient in isolation.

The implied return to experience is benchmarked against a small set of comparable studies on low-income women and maternal-employment policies, organized in a dedicated table that compares policy type, data source, population characteristics and estimated return across studies.

A back-of-envelope calculation translates the estimated earnings effect into an expected change in net income by incorporating taxes, transfers and child-care costs, explicitly framed as one input to a welfare assessment rather than a complete welfare accounting.
observations.quote: early work experience is likely to be financially advantageous

observations.statement: A footnote explicitly states that the precise policy mechanism generating the timing shift in post-birth work is not critical to interpreting the long-run effects, since only exogenous variation in work timing is required for the argument.
observations.quote: we only need exogenous variation in the timing of work after

observations.statement: Reliance on marital status and demographics measured at the CPS survey date rather than at first birth is explicitly acknowledged as a limitation, with a dedicated discussion of resulting bias directions and mitigating tests.

The conclusion explicitly cautions that higher earnings do not automatically mean early-exposed mothers are better off, since a complete welfare accounting would need information on work costs, lost leisure and spillovers to children that the paper does not measure.
observations.quote: information on other costs associated with work

observations.statement: The paper argues its temporary-incentive design generalizes beyond the EITC because several other common maternal work incentives share the same temporary, targeted structure, positioning the estimates as informative for a broader class of policies.

Findings are explicitly scoped to a low-income, largely young, working single-mother population in the United States, with the paper contrasting its population characteristics against other studies' settings in the closing comparison table.

The main employment, experience and earnings results are each presented as multi-panel event-study figures with confidence intervals, moving from a single-group plot to difference-in-differences and finally triple-difference coefficients.

Figure and table notes are written to be self-contained, each restating the control set, clustering level, data sources and sample-window definition rather than requiring the reader to cross-reference the main text.

A cross-comparison-group robustness figure plots each alternative comparison group's estimated coefficient and confidence interval against that group's own average outcome level, rather than presenting the alternatives only as a robustness table.

Supplementary tables and figures are consistently labeled with an A prefix and cited by number throughout the main text, but the online appendix document itself is not part of the provided source text.
observations.locator: throughout, e.g. online Appendix Table A.1

observations.statement: Summary statistics for the analysis sample are reported in a dedicated table, but that table is placed in the online appendix rather than in the main text.
observations.locator: Section II, Core Sample, cross-reference to online Appendix Table A.1

observations.statement: The introduction previews the qualitative pattern of the main findings, including the convergence of employment effects and the persistence of earnings effects, well before the empirical strategy section is introduced.

The introduction contains three explicit paragraphs positioning the paper relative to separate literatures: temporary work incentives after childbirth, returns to experience for low-income women, and long-run effects of safety-net programs.

The paper presents institutional background and the data section before the empirical strategy section, following a background-then-data-then-design ordering rather than opening directly with the estimating equation.

Robustness checks against the identification threats previewed earlier are consolidated into their own numbered section following the main results, rather than being interspersed within the results discussion.
Mechanism analysis is placed in its own section after both the main results and the robustness section, organized around a sequence of candidate channels considered one at a time.

The reference list includes a formal replication-data citation with its own DOI, distributed through an established data-repository intermediary rather than only hosted on a personal or journal website.
observations.locator: References, Kuka and Shenhav 2024 replication entry

observations.statement: Access to the underlying restricted administrative earnings data is described as having required agency assistance and a disclosure review process, acknowledged by name in the paper's front matter rather than in a formal data-availability statement.

The core dataset is constructed by linking public-use survey responses to restricted administrative earnings and vital-record files via a Census-assigned identifier, combining two distinct data-access regimes into one analysis file.

concordance.paper_says: Both employment and earnings equations are estimated by OLS regression of outcomes on treatment interactions and controls (equation 1, Section III).
concordance.card_shows: Specifications s1, s2 and s3 all record estimator=ols, command=reg (Stata regress via the xi: prefix).

concordance.paper_says: Equation (1) specifies birth-year-by-event-time, marital-status-by-event-time and birth-year-by-marital-status fixed effects plus individual and state-level controls interacted with marital status (Section III).
concordance.card_shows: s1/s2 fixed_effects field lists only ['yearfb','gr_yrs_fr_fb']; the richer marital-interaction terms appear in the ddd_base binding and s2's resolved_call rather than in the structured fixed_effects field.
concordance.note: Structured field captures two of the three named fixed-effect dimensions; marital-interaction terms are visible in the raw formula but not parsed out.

concordance.paper_says: Standard errors are clustered at the state level throughout the paper (Section III).
concordance.card_shows: se.cluster_level=['statefip'] recorded identically for specifications s1, s2 and s3.

concordance.paper_says: Beyond state-clustered standard errors, the paper also reports randomization-inference confidence intervals as an alternative inference approach (Section III; Section V).
concordance.card_shows: The card's only diagnostic entry, x1, is a pretrend_test with status unknown; no randomization-inference record exists anywhere in the card.

concordance.paper_says: The core sample is restricted by a maximum interview age, a minimum age at first birth, and membership in one of two birth-cohort exposure windows, in addition to being matched to SSA earnings (Section II).
concordance.card_shows: pipeline.sample_restrictions lists a single entry, description 'SSA matched', attached to spec s1; the age and birth-cohort-window restrictions described in the paper are not separately recorded.

concordance.paper_says: Married mothers are the primary comparison group, with childless and lower-earning women used as alternative comparison groups in robustness checks (Section IIIA; Section V).
concordance.card_shows: comparison_group is null in design d1 and null in every specification s1-s3.

concordance.paper_says: State-level policy controls include the unemployment rate, minimum wage, AFDC/TANF benefit level, Medicaid generosity, six welfare-waiver indicators, a TANF/waiver indicator and a 2009 EITC reform indicator, each allowed to vary by marital status (Section III).
concordance.card_shows: s2's resolved_call lists an extensive married-interacted control set (urate, minwage, afdcmax4, medthresh, missmedthresh, reform, tl, jobs_ex, jobs_sanc, disr, famcap, work_tl, yr09plus, a_age) matching the paper's described controls, though controls_summary itself is left null.

concordance.paper_says: The main empirical strategy section does not mention using analytic or sampling weights in the regression specification.
concordance.card_shows: s1, s2 and s3 all record weights='aw=num', an analytic weight by a variable named num.

concordance.paper_says: Pre-trend behavior is checked by inspecting pre-birth event-study coefficients for the single-group, DD and DDD models, reported as flat and close to zero (Section IV; Figure 2).
concordance.card_shows: diagnostic x1 is kind=pretrend_test with status=unknown, noting only that pre-birth coefficients in the event study show treatment timing.

concordance.paper_says: Section V describes an extensive robustness battery: alternative comparison groups, calendar-year event studies, alternative economic-condition controls, additional specification checks, alternative sample restrictions, and randomization inference.
concordance.card_shows: The card's top-level robustness array is empty; only specification s3 is separately flagged role=robustness, covering a single simple difference-in-differences check on the never-married subsample.

concordance.paper_says: The main text presents three numbered tables (employment/experience/earnings, CPS hours, and a policy comparison table) and five numbered figures.
concordance.card_shows: outputs.tables contains a single entry, t1 (table1.tex), tied to specification s1; outputs.figures is empty.

concordance.paper_says: The analysis links Social Security Detailed Earnings Records and Numident files to Current Population Survey responses, supplemented by SIPP marital histories and published state-level policy series (Section II).
concordance.card_shows: data[] lists a CPS survey source and two restricted administrative sources (Numident, and a second admin source referencing cps_newder consistent with SSA earnings records); SIPP and the state-policy series are not separately recorded, consistent with the card's partial coverage.

gaps: No preregistration, IRB approval, or ethics statement appears anywhere in the main text (preregistration_or_ethics category not observed).
No explicit discussion of a few-clusters problem or wild-bootstrap inference is given for the state-level clustering, despite randomization inference being offered as an alternative.
No formal multiple-testing correction is described despite testing many outcome variables and several alternative comparison groups across Sections IV-V.
The Online Appendix, referenced very frequently for supporting figures, tables and derivations, is a separate document not included in the provided source text and could not be read.
The recipe card's only diagnostic entry (x1, pretrend_test) is marked status=unknown even though the paper reports and plots pre-trend results directly in the main text.

The recipe card's robustness array is empty and its outputs record only one of three main tables and none of the five figures, reflecting the card's partial code-reading scope rather than the paper's own reporting.
No software name (e.g., Stata) is stated in the main text; the xi: command usage recorded in the card comes only from the replication code, not from paper text.

reading.note: Read all 31 pages of the extracted text in full: title/abstract, introduction, institutional background (Section I), data (Section II), estimation strategy and identification assumptions (Section III), main results (Section IV), robustness (Section V), mechanisms and policy comparison (Section VI), conclusion (Section VII), and the reference list. The paper's Online Appendix, cited extensively for supplementary figures, tables and derivations, is a separate document not included in this source text and was not read; observations describing appendix content rely on the main text's own description of what the appendix contains.
